sections.overview: The Jack Snipe is a secretive migratory wader and a winter visitor to Britain.
sections.identification: At 17–19 cm long, it is smaller and shorter-billed than the Common Snipe, Gallinago gallinago, and often crouches in cover until approached closely.
sections.habitat: It breeds in wet grassland, bogs and marshes in northern Europe and Russia, then uses vegetated wetlands and flooded ground during migration and winter.
sections.diet: Its food includes adult and larval insects, worms, small snails, and some seeds and aquatic plant material.
sections.behavior: When flushed, it usually makes a short, low flight and drops back into cover, unlike the Common Snipe’s more conspicuous zigzag escape.
sections.reproduction: The usual clutch has four eggs, incubated by the female. It breeds in the far north during the warmer months.
sections.ecology: Its camouflage and habit of remaining motionless make it easy to overlook, so British records may understate how often it occurs.
sections.conservation: The current BTO account lists it as globally Least Concern, while the LPO identifies wetland loss and degradation and lead poisoning as pressures.
